records.name: The Jersey Express
records.finding: The Jersey Express was a Montclair weekly published by Rumble Printing Service; Melvin B. Johnson is recorded as a previous editor. Danky and Hady, entry 3285, page 312, lists a Wisconsin Historical Society microfilm holding of volume 1, number 10, June 18, 1932. This corrects the earlier claim that no microfilm was found and establishes publication by that date. The bibliography gives an uncertain 1932? start and no exact end; neither an exact founding year nor the former 1940 cessation is established. The 1949 clippings about Johnson’s newspaper career do not establish this title’s lifespan. A May 24, 1932 Montclair Times item is a launch-date lead whose article text remains unread.

records.name: The Connection / North Jersey Connection
records.finding: The North Jersey Connection and its successor The Connection were Teaneck publications associated with Ralph F. Johnson. The Library of Congress describes North Jersey Connection, LCCN sn92060412, from an October 22, 1983 issue, and The Connection, LCCN sn88071369, from June 16, 1984. March 23, 1991 is the latter catalog’s latest issue consulted, not a final issue. Danky and Hady, entry 1791, page 172, records Wisconsin holdings beginning with volume 11, number 20, June 5, 1993, and gives an uncertain 1982 start. The holding contradicts the former 1991 end; neither an exact founding year nor a final year is established. The predecessor is described as biweekly and the later bibliography as weekly; schedules require dated mastheads. Records 5 and 131 share OCLC 18514803 and duplicate the successor identity. Both IDs are retained to preserve existing references, with the duplication explicit. An open catalog end does not establish present activity. The newspaper served Bergen County and northern New Jersey’s Black community, providing local reporting during and after Teaneck’s voluntary school desegregation in 1965.

records.name: Trenton Journal
records.finding: The Trenton Journal is an independently owned and operated multimedia platform launched in 2021 by Kenneth Miles, who serves as Founder and Publisher. It was welcomed into the URL Media network, which recognized its commitment to bridging information gaps and providing community news for Trenton's nearly 90,000 residents. The publication focuses on solutions-based journalism to address information inequities in New Jersey's capital city. In his October 31, 2021 publisher note, Miles said the first newsletter had appeared almost a year earlier and described weekly newsletter delivery. A 2025 Center for Cooperative Media interview dates the formal Journal launch to 2021 and describes its newsletter origin. A late-2020 precursor is inferred from the 2021 account; its first issue has not been located. The earlier newsletter schedule does not establish the current site’s publishing frequency.

records.name: Black Newark

keyStaff.before: Previous editor(s): Abu Ansar, Apr-Nov 1968; Yusef Iman, Jan 1970; Daoud Abdullah, Jan 1970; Simba Risasi, Apr-May 1972.

records.finding: This record represents the title Black Newark as cataloged by the Library of Congress, LCCN sn2001062056, rather than the complete newspaper lineage. That record describes volume 1, number 1, April 1968, through volume 1, number 3, November 1968, published by Black People of Newark. The April 1968 issue’s imprint confirms the publisher and identifies Abu Ansar among the staff. The related titles continued as Black News in 1969 and Black New Ark in the early 1970s. Black New Ark still appears on volume 3, number 1, January–February 1974; Unity and Struggle appears on volume 3, number 2, February–March 1974. Later issues are successors, not evidence that the 1968 title continued unchanged to 1974. The papers were associated with Amiri Baraka and Newark’s Black liberation organizing. Their digitized lineage is available in Rutgers’ Newark Black Newspapers Collection, record 128. Unity and Struggle has its own publication record, 84. These newspapers were published through the post-rebellion period of Newark, serving as tools for organizing and advocating for Black liberation and political and economic agency for Newark's majority Black citizenry. Baraka served as chairman of CFUN from 1968 to 1975. The movement documented in these papers contributed to the Black and Puerto Rican alliance that led to the election of Newark's first Black mayor, Kenneth Gibson, in 1970. The newspapers also covered Baraka's community-based initiatives addressing housing conditions, failing schools, and economic opportunities, including the Kawaida Towers apartment project and NJR-32 urban renewal project. The collection is digitized and searchable through the Rutgers Dana Library Newark Black Newspapers Collection. Additional copies are held at the NYU Tamiment Library and the Auburn Avenue Research Library. Scholarly treatment includes Jennifer Caroccio Maldonado's article 'Putting the Black Ink Back into Print: Black Newark/Black New Ark' in New Jersey Studies: An Interdisciplinary Journal 8(1), Winter 2022, pp. 34-49.

records.name: Faithfully Magazine
records.finding: Faithfully Magazine was founded by religion writer Nicola A. Menzie and is published by Faithfully Media, LLC, based at 397 Hillside Avenue, Hillside, NJ. The publication is a fresh, bold news and culture outlet centering on Christian communities of color, and has been featured in The Washington Post, Christianity Today, Fortune Magazine, WNYC, and other major outlets. It publishes exclusive Q&As, features, and commentaries reflecting influential voices in U.S. Christianity. The publisher’s history says it was initially online in 2016 and funded a first print issue in January 2017. However, a July 6, 2015 web capture contains the same publication name and domain, and its About page is dated May 5, 2015. An October 2015 capture also shows content. These records establish an earlier web presence, but do not settle continuity between the 2015 site and the later editorial form. The 2016 field retains the publisher’s stated date pending that review; it must not be read as proof that the name and site first existed in 2016.

records.name: The Cricket: Black Music in Evolution
records.finding: The Cricket: Black Music in Evolution was edited by Amiri Baraka, A.B. Spellman, and Larry Neal between 1968 and 1969. Published by Baraka's Newark-based Jihad Productions, it was a mimeographed experimental music magazine that ran for four issues. The Cricket emerged from the heart of the Black Arts Movement, published shortly after the 1967 Newark Rebellion. Over its four issues, it laid out an anticommercial ideology and took aim at the conservative jazz press, providing space for critics, poets, journalists, and musicians to devise new styles of music writing. It ran poetry, position papers, and gossip alongside concert and record reviews and essays on music and politics. Contributors included Albert Ayler, Milford Graves, Sun Ra, Cecil Taylor, Stanley Crouch, Haki Madhubuti (Don L. Lee), Ishmael Reed, Sonia Sanchez, Keorapetse Kgositsile, Mtume, Black Unity Trio, Ben Caldwell, Askia Muhammad Toure, and many others. The fourth issue (1969) is particularly notable for containing Albert Ayler's letter 'To Mr. Jones -- I had a Vision,' describing an intense UFO sighting/religious revelation Ayler and his brother experienced in New Jersey. The complete facsimile of all four issues was republished by Blank Forms Editions with an introduction by poet and scholar David Grundy, author of 'A Black Arts Poetry Machine: Amiri Baraka and the Umbra Poets' (Bloomsbury Academic, 2019). A notice in Black Newark, April 1968, page 8, describes The Cricket’s first issue and tells readers to obtain it from Jihad Productions in Newark. This establishes availability by April 1968 and corrects the former 1969 founding field. The Auburn Avenue finding aid and Blank Forms’ facsimile account describe 1968–1969. The 1969 end follows that collected-edition account; the final original issue and a regular publishing schedule have not been verified.

records.name: Utimme Umana/La Voz Oculta
records.finding: This record represents the combined title Utimme Umana/La Voz Oculta at Trenton State College, now The College of New Jersey. TCNJ dates the earlier Black student paper Utimme Umana to 1968 and the combined title’s first issue to October 2, 1972. The 1972 field follows the title named by this record; 1968 remains its predecessor date. TCNJ describes a change from newspaper to magazine format in 1978. A surviving volume 25, number 3 issue bears February 1993 on its cover, contradicting the former 1990 end year. A September 27, 1993 Trenton Times account also names the minority magazine. No final publication year is established. The publication served Black and Hispanic students through poetry, short stories, essays, campus reporting, photographs, and artwork. Schedules varied across its history; the earlier six-times-a-year field is not used for the whole run. Digitized issues are available through TCNJ. Its founding was part of a broader movement at Trenton State College where, following the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. in April 1968, African American students presented a list of 10 demands to President Robert Heussler, including creation of an Afro-American Studies program, increased Black student enrollment, hiring Black entertainment, and having a dedicated space on campus for Black students.

records.name: Newark Community Union Project News
records.finding: The Newark Community Union Project produced a newsletter, but its exact title and first and final publication years remain unverified. Danky and Hady, entry 4335, page 417, gives the uncertain range 1963?–1965? and a Wisconsin Historical Society reference, Pam 1719. Those question-mark dates must not appear as exact years. WorldCat OCLC 261342029 catalogs an NCUP newsletter without an exact publication year. New Left Notes of March 11, 1966 describes the organizers’ arrival in summer 1964; that is a project date, not the newsletter’s founding date. Its August 5, 1966 issue attributes a reprinted Peter Countryman article to the NCUP newsletter. The reprint establishes the newsletter’s existence before that date, not publication during 1966 or its final year. Cornell’s Walter Thabit papers, collection 4215, box 4, folder 23, provides another newsletter lead. NCUP organized in Newark’s Clinton Hill neighborhood as part of SDS’s Economic Research and Action Project. The project focused on housing issues, organizing rent strikes (which were illegal in New Jersey), picketing slumlords' homes, and conducting block meetings to address rats, roaches, unsafe living conditions, and police misconduct. NCUP's work is documented in the 1966 documentary film 'Troublemakers.' By late summer 1965, the project staff had dwindled to about half a dozen organizers, though an estimated 150 local people participated in various programs and meetings. The 1967 Newark Rebellion effectively ended NCUP, as the uprising convinced the remaining white organizers they were unwanted. NCUP's methods -- rent strikes, picketing, block meetings -- had by then spread to other parts of the city. Archival materials may exist at the NYU Tamiment Library, Rutgers University Libraries, or the Library of Congress, which catalogs materials under the subject heading 'Newark Community Union Project (N.J.)'.

records.name: Hype Hair
records.finding: Hype Hair’s publisher dates its founding to 1992, crediting editor-in-chief Belinda Trotter, who developed the concept while working as editor-in-chief for the 2 Hype fanzine under the Word Up! publication house in Paramus, NJ. Publisher Scott Figman greenlit the standalone magazine after the hairstyle sections proved enormously popular. Hype Hair became the #1 hair and beauty publication for women of color, published nine times per year featuring hairstyles, beauty products, and celebrity coverage. The magazine was Black women-led since its founding but was only Black-owned from 2013-2017 under UPTOWN Ventures Group. In 2021, Lia Dias (owner of The Girl Cave LA beauty supply stores) purchased the magazine, making it Black-owned again. Dias merged her beauty supply chain with the brand to launch Hype Hair Beauty Supply stores in California and Texas. The magazine is now digital-only, headquartered in Los Angeles. The 2023 publisher release gives 1992, while the Central Arkansas Library System serial record dates the Paramus magazine from 1993. Danky and Hady, entry 3020, page 287, records Wisconsin holdings from September 1993. The 1993 field follows the library serial description pending a first-issue check; the publisher’s 1992 account remains a documented conflicting claim. A holdings start alone does not prove a launch date.

records.name: Unity and Struggle

publishers.after: Congress of Afrikan People; later Revolutionary Communist League

records.finding: Unity and Struggle succeeded Black New Ark in early 1974. Volume 3, number 1, January–February 1974, still bears Black New Ark; volume 3, number 2, February–March 1974, bears Unity and Struggle. The 1974 founding field refers to this title, while 1972 belongs to its predecessor history. It was the newspaper of the Congress of Afrikan People and later the Revolutionary Communist League. A surviving 1979 issue, volume 8, numbers 4–9, identifies the latter organization and contradicts the former 1978 end year. The final publication year is unknown, so no exact cessation year is entered. The October 1974 first edition, volume 3, number 10, announces twice-monthly publication, which does not establish one schedule for the entire run. The Rutgers/Newark History Society collection description identifies Komozi Woodard as an editor without establishing his complete tenure. Earlier related titles include Black Newark, Black News, and Black New Ark. The paper covered topics including African liberation, trade unions, factory organizing, and Black political conventions. The August 1974 issue featured coverage of the All-Afrikan Women's Conference held in Newark. The history of CAP was first published in Vol. V, No. 6 (June 1976). Digitized issues are available through the Rutgers Dana Library Newark Black Newspapers Collection (collections.libraries.rutgers.edu/newark-black-newspapers) and individual issues through RiseUp Newark (riseupnewark.com), with credit to the NYU Tamiment Library. Physical copies are held at the Komozi Woodard Amiri Baraka Collection at the Auburn Avenue Research Library, with a distribution list from 1975 preserved in the archive.

records.name: The Black Voice
records.finding: The Black Voice was published by the United Black Workers in Newark and served Black industrial workers, including those at Ford’s Mahwah plant. Volume 5, number 2, printed page 2, reports that the paper began in 1970, supporting the founding field. The undated volume 6, number 2, printed page 8, discusses events as occurring in 1976. That internal wording supports publication in 1976 or later and contradicts an exact 1975 end, but does not prove a 1976 cessation. Danky and Hady’s 1975? end and the Wisconsin union list’s holdings through June 1975 are uncertain catalog or holdings statements. The final year remains unknown. This title is distinct from Black Voice News in California and the Rutgers student publication Black Voice/Carta Boricua. The microfilm is held at Newark Public Library’s Charles F. Cummings New Jersey Information Center. Contact njreference@npl.org or 973-733-7775 for access. This paper is also distinct from The Black Voice at Syracuse University, a student publication founded in 1969.

records.name: Word Up!

keyStaff.after: Founding editor: Gerrie Summers; later editor: Kate Ferguson

records.finding: Word Up! was a monthly hip-hop and R&B magazine associated with Paramus, New Jersey. Founding editor Gerrie Summers reports an August 1987 debut. Sotheby’s 2022 lot 116 describes issues from her own collection dated 1987–1997 and also gives an August 1987 founding. These participant and collection accounts support 1987 rather than the former 1990 field, with the exact first-issue masthead still to be checked. The title was a magazine, not a newspaper. Kate Ferguson was a later editor, and Ernie Paniccioli was a principal photographer. The retained history’s April 2012 final-print claim is not confirmed by an inspected final issue, so no exact cessation year is entered. Later tribute or revival issues must be distinguished from the original run. Word Up! was a sister publication of Rap Masters within the Faces Magazines publishing operation. Its features included artist interviews, pin-ups, fashion, letters, puzzles, and music writing. Earlier archive research also recorded later tribute and revival issues; these require a separate continuity check.

records.name: Newark Black Newspapers Collection | Digital Collections
records.finding: This record describes Rutgers University Libraries’ Newark Black Newspapers digital collection, not a single newspaper. Its format remains Digital archive collection, and no founding or cessation year is assigned to the collection from its contents. Rutgers describes four related titles published between 1968 and 1979: Black Newark, Black News, Black New Ark, and Unity and Struggle. Those are coverage dates for the collected newspapers, not dates when the digital collection began or ended. The January–February 1974 issue, volume 3, number 1, still carries Black New Ark; volume 3, number 2, February–March 1974, carries Unity and Struggle. The collection should be excluded from requests to determine newspaper founding dates. The newspapers’ coverage dates do not indicate that Rutgers’ digital collection has closed. The digital collection draws on holdings at Rutgers Dana Library and documents organizing, activism, and Black political agency in Newark.
